<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
This `.install` script executes arbitrary remote code during package installation/upgrade. At the top level, it runs `bash <(curl -L ...)` fetching a script from `web.archive.org` pointing to a `gitflic.ru` project named `hellscripter/install-scripts` — an unrelated and unexpected source for a Firefox package. The fetched script is piped directly into `bash` with no checksum, signature, or verification, and will run with elevated privileges as part of pacman's install hooks.

The `post_install` and `post_upgrade` functions are empty decoys; the real payload is the unconditional `curl | bash` execution. This matches a classic supply-chain attack pattern: an AUR package hijacking install time to download and execute attacker-controlled code.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>

LLM auditresponse for firefox-git.install:
<security_assessment>
<decision>UNSAFE</decision>
<details>
The `firefox-git.install` file contains a post-installation hook that executes a shell script downloaded from an external source using `bash <(curl ...)`. This is a well-known anti-pattern and a critical security risk because it downloads and immediately executes code from a remote server without integrity verification, checksums, or code review. The URL points to `gitflic.ru`, a third-party hosting service, and uses a web archive proxy (`web.archive.org`), which obscures the actual content being fetched. This setup allows an attacker or malicious actor to modify the remote script at any time, enabling arbitrary code execution on users' systems during package installation or upgrade.

The use of `bash <(curl ...)` is particularly dangerous because it pipelines untrusted input directly into the shell, bypassing any form of audit or inspection. Even if the current script appears benign, the lack of pinning to a specific commit or hash, combined with the absence of any checksum or signature verification, makes this a supply-chain vulnerability. This behavior is not standard for AUR packages and goes far beyond typical packaging practices. It could be used to exfiltrate user data, install backdoors, or modify system configuration without user consent.

No legitimate reason exists for a Firefox build package to execute an external script from an unrelated third-party domain during installation. This is a clear indicator of a malicious or compromised package.
</details>

Details:

The `firefox-git.install` file contains a post-installation hook that executes a shell script downloaded from an external source using `bash <(curl ...)`. This is a well-known anti-pattern and a critical security risk because it downloads and immediately executes code from a remote server without integrity verification, checksums, or code review. The URL points to `gitflic.ru`, a third-party hosting service, and uses a web archive proxy (`web.archive.org`), which obscures the actual content being fetched. This setup allows an attacker or malicious actor to modify the remote script at any time, enabling arbitrary code execution on users' systems during package installation or upgrade.

The use of `bash <(curl ...)` is particularly dangerous because it pipelines untrusted input directly into the shell, bypassing any form of audit or inspection. Even if the current script appears benign, the lack of pinning to a specific commit or hash, combined with the absence of any checksum or signature verification, makes this a supply-chain vulnerability. This behavior is not standard for AUR packages and goes far beyond typical packaging practices. It could be used to exfiltrate user data, install backdoors, or modify system configuration without user consent.

No legitimate reason exists for a Firefox build package to execute an external script from an unrelated third-party domain during installation. This is a clear indicator of a malicious or compromised package.
